ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT Act); Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism (Definitions) Regulations 2011; Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism (Acceptable Sources of Funding) Regulations 2011; Companies Act 1993; Companies (Register of Ultimate Beneficial Ownership) Amendment Act 2023; the Financial Markets Authority AML/CFT supervisory framework; the Reserve Bank of New Zealand AML/CFT codes; and the Privacy Act 2020 for personal data protection in due diligence.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Registrar of Companies, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (New Zealand Companies Office)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: obtain the electronic certificate, print and have the printout certified by a New Zealand notary public, then affix an apostille certificate from the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT). Consular legalization is not used because New Zealand is a party to the Hague Apostille Convention; apostille and consular legalization are mutually exclusive and must never be chained sequentially.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: request the Certificate of Good Standing from the Companies Office, notarize the certificate if required by the destination registry, then apply to MFAT for an apostille. No consular legalization is required; the apostille route is the sole valid authentication path for New Zealand-origin documents in Apostille Convention states.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Board Resolution and Power of Attorney
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Board of Directors of the proposed New Zealand company or the authorised incorporating shareholder
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: execute the board resolution before a New Zealand notary public who attests the directors' signatures, then obtain an MFAT apostille. The notarial certificate and apostille are sufficient; consular legalization is not applicable and must not be added.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Founding shareholders and directors, adopted at incorporation and filed with the New Zealand Companies Office
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: have the final consolidated Articles of Association certified as a true copy by a New Zealand notary public, then apply to MFAT for an apostille. Apostille and consular legalization are mutually exclusive; no chain of apostille followed by consular legalization is permitted.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: A New Zealand registered bank under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989 at which the company holds or will hold its operational account
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille path: the bank's authorized signatory signs the reference letter, the signature is notarized by a New Zealand notary public, and the notarized letter receives an apostille from MFAT. If the bank refuses notarization, the bank letter may be accompanied by a solicitors certification from New Zealand corporate counsel and apostilled; consular legalization is not used for Apostille Convention counterparties.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: All ultimate beneficial owners, directors, and authorized signatories must be screened before incorporation against the New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Unit watchlist, the OFAC SDN list and sectoral sanction lists, the UN Security Council consolidated sanctions list, and the sanctions lists of Australia, the United Kingdom, and the European Union. Any politically exposed person triggers enhanced due diligence covering source of wealth, source of funds, professional background, and family or close associate relationships. Every positive screening hit requires immediate escalation to the AML/CFT compliance officer, a full risk assessment, and, where required, a suspicious activity report to the New Zealand Financial Intelligence Unit. Screening must be repeated continuously through sanctions screening software and refreshed no later than 24 hours before incorporation.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office online portal and New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) register, accessible at https://companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz/
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Under the Companies Act 1993, company names may be in English or te reo Maori but must be expressed in Latin script for the NZBN register. Non-Latin script names must be phonetically transliterated into English or Maori before registration. The proposed name must be capable of accurate electronic searching, must not exceed the permitted character limit, and must contain the mandatory Limited, Ltd, or equivalent legal suffix. Four-tier naming review examines distinguishability, prohibited tokens, restricted tokens, and misrepresentation.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Within 20 working days after a name rejection notice, the applicant may file a written reconsideration request with the Registrar of Companies using the original Companies Office account, stating the statutory grounds for approval, explaining why the name is not identical or confusingly similar to an existing name, why it is not misleading, and attaching written consent from any ministry or regulator if a restricted word is involved. The Registrar must issue a reconsideration decision; if the rejection is affirmed, the applicant may appeal to the High Court on judicial review grounds within 20 working days. A successful appeal or administrative reversal causes the name to be reserved for an additional 20 working days.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office is permissible only if it provides a physical street address in New Zealand, is not a PO Box, is staffed during normal business hours, and is capable of receiving service of legal process. Under section 187 of the Companies Act 1993, the registered office must be accessible to the public. For a digital video game publisher using Steam and PlayStation Store, a virtual office with mail handling and meeting room facilities will generally satisfy the Companies Office, but the Inland Revenue Department and New Zealand banks will reject a purely nominal virtual office for tax residence and bank account purposes if the board and majority of management operate offshore. The company must maintain one local director, a local registered agent, adequate minutes and director decisions, and financial records physically in New Zealand. A commercial mailbox without human presence is not an acceptable registered office.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Checklist: (1) registered office nameplate or accessible reception; (2) physical corporate records and minute book available at the registered office; (3) local director contactable during business hours; (4) UBO register maintained or held by the registered agent; (5) financial statements and GST records in New Zealand; (6) bank account information accessible from the registered office; (7) no outward indication of a mere mail-forwarding facility. Quantified risk: Low-Risk at 3% to 5% annual probability for a standard low-risk digital publisher with full record compliance. If the company uses a high-density shared virtual office or a commercial mailbox address, the likelihood of an unannounced physical inspection by the New Zealand Companies Office or Inland Revenue rises to between 15% and 25% annually.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand), particularly sections 5 (Incorporation), 13 (Application for registration), 14 (Certificate of incorporation), 15 (Constitution), 16 (Share capital), 17 (Allotment of shares), 18 (Consideration for allotment), 19 (Share certificates), 20 (Register of shares), 21 (Share transfers), 22 (Shareholder rights), 23 (Directors), 24 (Appointment of directors), 25 (Duties of directors), 26 (Meetings of directors), 27 (Board resolutions), 28 (Registered office), 29 (Company records), 30 (Financial reporting), 31 (Annual return), 32 (Offences), 33 (Penalties), 34 (Regulations)
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (a business unit of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment)
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Form NZCN - Application for Registration of a Company, together with any constitution and consent to act as director/shareholder forms
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: None. The Companies Act 1993 does not prescribe a minimum paid-up capital for a limited company. The company may be incorporated with zero or nominal share capital, but must have at least one share issued and allotted. There is no requirement for a blocked escrow account.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en:
RESOLUTION OF THE FIRST MEETING OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF [COMPANY NAME] LIMITED (the "Company")

Pursuant to the Companies Act 1993 (the "Act") and the Constitution of the Company (if adopted), the following resolutions were duly passed at the first meeting of the Board of Directors held on [date] at [place] at [time].

1. INCORPORATION AND REGISTRATION: RESOLVED that the incorporation of the Company under the Act be and is hereby ratified and confirmed, and that the Certificate of Incorporation issued by the New Zealand Companies Office be accepted and filed in the Company's statutory records.

2. ADOPTION OF CONSTITUTION: RESOLVED that the Constitution of the Company, as presented to this meeting, be and is hereby adopted as the Constitution of the Company, and that the same be filed with the Companies Office in accordance with section 15 of the Act.

3. ALLOTMENT OF SHARES: RESOLVED that the shares of the Company be and are hereby allotted as follows: [list subscribers and number of shares] to the persons named and addressed in the register of members, and that the consideration for such allotment be [cash or property or services] as set out in the allotment documents, and that the Board be and is hereby authorized to issue share certificates accordingly.

4. APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTORS: RESOLVED that the following persons be and are hereby appointed as directors of the Company: [names], each of whom has consented to act as a director and has signed the consent form as required by section 17 of the Act.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Name Availability Search and Pre-Incorporation Preparation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a name availability search on the New Zealand Companies Office website. If the desired name is available, it is recommended to reserve it for a fee of NZD 10 (optional). Prepare the company constitution (if any) and ensure the full legal names, addresses, and dates of birth of all proposed directors and shareholders are collected. Verify that each director is eligible under the Companies Act 1993, being at least 18 years old and not disqualified. Confirm that the registered office address will be a physical address in New Zealand, not a post office box. Ensure that the intended business activities (ISIC 5820 - software publishing) are lawful and do not require special licensing. Compile all required information and documents for the online application to avoid queries.
required_dossiers: Full names, addresses, and dates of birth of directors and shareholders
Consent forms for directors and shareholders
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is rejected, select an alternative name and resubmit. If a director is disqualified, replace them with a qualified individual.

step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete the online application for registration of a company (Form NZCN) on the Companies Office website. Provide the company name, registered office address, details of directors and shareholders, share structure, and any constitution. Attach the consent forms and any other required documents. Pay the incorporation fee of NZD 150 using a credit card or online payment. Review the application for accuracy and submit it. The Companies Office will process the application and, if satisfied, issue a Certificate of Incorporation electronically. The company is incorporated on the date of registration. After incorporation, the company must maintain a register of members and other statutory records. The certificate of incorporation must be retained as proof of legal existence.
required_dossiers: Consent forms for directors and shareholders
Proof of identity for directors (passport or driver's license)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried, respond to the Companies Office within 5 working days with the requested information. If the application is rejected, correct the errors and resubmit.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Post-Incorporation Formalities and Bank Account Opening
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Company's board of directors and commercial bank
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After incorporation, the initial directors must convene a first board meeting to formally adopt the constitution (if not already), allot shares to subscribers, appoint officers, and fix the registered office. The board must pass the first board resolution as per the pro-forma template. Subsequently, open a corporate bank account with a New Zealand bank. Provide the bank with the certificate of incorporation, constitution, board resolution authorizing the account, and identification of signatories. The bank will conduct due diligence and may request additional information. Once the account is opened, issue share certificates to shareholders and maintain the company's statutory registers. Ensure that all company records are kept at the registered office address.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the bank rejects the account application, provide additional documentation or choose another bank. If the board resolution is defective, pass a new resolution.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) and New Zealand Companies Office
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Register the company for an IRD number (tax file number) with the Inland Revenue Department. This can be done online via the IRD website. Provide the company's legal name, registration number, and business activity details. If the company expects to have an annual turnover exceeding NZD 60,000, register for GST. Also, register for PAYE if the company will have employees. For a digital publishing business, no special industry license is required. Additionally, ensure that the company files its annual return with the Companies Office each year. The company must also comply with the Financial Reporting Act 2013 if it is a large company. This step ensures full tax compliance and avoids penalties.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the IRD number is delayed, contact IRD for assistance. If the company fails to register for GST when required, penalties may apply; register as soon as possible.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Inland Revenue / Te Tari Taake), official online portal myIR at https://myir.ird.govt.nz; New Zealand Customs Service for border/export controls
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: For the NZ_LTD, the standard path is: 1. Incorporate the New Zealand limited company with the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act 1993; the New Zealand Companies Office issues the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN), and Inland Revenue assigns the IRD number for income tax and GST purposes, with confirmation available through myIR. 2. If instead the operating entity is a foreign non-resident company carrying on a taxable activity in New Zealand, apply to Inland Revenue for the Non-Resident Company IRD registration using the Commissioner's statutory non-resident company registration procedure; this requires the foreign certificate of incorporation, details of the New Zealand fixed establishment or agent, director particulars, and overseas tax identification where applicable. 3. Register for GST through myIR under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 when actual or expected taxable supplies exceed or are likely to exceed NZD 60,000 in any 12-month period; voluntary registration is also available. 4. If physical goods will be exported, obtain a Customs client/trader reference from the New Zealand Customs Service and lodge valid export entries through the Trade Single Window or Integrated Cargo System. 5. Maintain the share register and any non-resident ownership documentation for income tax residence, imputation, and non-resident withholding tax compliance.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: None; New Zealand has no check-the-box entity classification election. An NZ limited company is statutorily taxed at entity level at 28%, cannot elect pass-through treatment, and the hybrid mismatch rules in the Income Tax Act 2007 are mandatory rather than elective.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 in actual or estimated taxable supplies in any 12-month period; the same NZD 60,000 threshold applies to non-resident suppliers of remote services/electronically supplied services sold to New Zealand consumers.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: New Zealand does not impose real-time fiscal clearance, mandatory e-invoicing, or an anti-fraud digital stamping regime. Valid GST tax invoices must include the prescribed details under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 and be issued within 28 days of supply; electronic tax invoices are permitted. Voluntary PEPPOL e-invoicing may be used for business-to-government transactions. GST returns and payments are filed electronically through myIR, with no mandatory transaction-level API clearance.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985, a supply is zero-rated when the statutory export test is met. For this video game publishing business: (i) services supplied to a non-resident person who is outside New Zealand at the time the services are performed are zero-rated; (ii) remote or electronically supplied digital publishing services provided to offshore platform operators such as Valve/Steam or PlayStation Store are zero-rated where the supplier does not know or have reason to believe the recipient is present in New Zealand and the service is performed outside New Zealand; (iii) physical goods exported from New Zealand, such as promotional or collector physical merchandise, are zero-rated only if there is a valid Customs export entry and evidence of actual departure from New Zealand; and (iv) supplies made to New Zealand consumers or to any person that acquires the service for direct consumption in New Zealand remain taxable at 15%. The mere selection of a foreign digital store platform does not by itself create zero-rating; the recipient, place of supply, and consumption location must be substantiated.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Entry accepted by the New Zealand Customs Service under the Customs and Excise Act 2018, lodged through the Trade Single Window or Integrated Cargo System, for physical goods exports
Bill of Lading or Air Waybill evidencing physical departure of goods from New Zealand and delivery to a foreign destination, for physical exports only

Commercial invoice, digital publishing agreement, or platform revenue statement with Valve/Steam or PlayStation Store identifying the non-resident platform operator and the consideration for the exported offshore service

Bank credit advice, SWIFT MT103, or foreign exchange settlement advice from a New Zealand bank showing receipt of the overseas platform payout; New Zealand does not issue a formal Inward Remittance Certificate (FIRC)

Recipient non-resident status evidence for digital services, including registered business address, jurisdiction of incorporation, payment billing address, IP address geo-location data, and platform user or merchant metadata supporting performance and consumption outside New Zealand
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: New Zealand does not impose a general statutory 180-day foreign exchange repatriation deadline for GST purposes; the 180-day figure should be read as an internal audit-evidence benchmark. Inland Revenue may claw back a zero-rated export if the supplier cannot produce the required export entry, contemporaneous transport documents, non-resident service evidence, or foreign exchange receipt evidence. Unsubstantiated zero-rating is reassessed as taxable at 15% at the time of supply, with use-of-money interest under the Tax Administration Act 1994. Civil shortfall penalties may be imposed from 20% for failure to take reasonable care up to 150% for evasion; false export declarations and materially incorrect records can also be prosecuted under the Customs and Excise Act 2018 and the Tax Administration Act 1994. All export evidence and underlying transactional records must be retained in New Zealand for at least seven years.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Pūtea Matua)
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand operates a fully liberalised capital and current account. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989 and the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 define the regulatory perimeter, but the Reserve Bank of New Zealand does not issue exchange-control permits for ordinary trade, service royalties, or equity flows. The New Zealand dollar is freely convertible; no central-bank prior approval is required for inbound share capital, outbound dividends, intercompany loan repayments, or Steam and PlayStation royalty remittances. The Overseas Investment Act 2005 applies only to sensitive land, significant business assets, and fishing quota; a pure digital games publishing entity without such assets will not trigger OIO consent. Profit repatriation is governed by Companies Act 1993 solvency and dividend distribution rules, with non-resident withholding tax at the applicable double-tax agreement rate. Banks perform source-of-funds and sanctions checks but do not enforce conversion ratios or repatriation timelines. Unlike jurisdictions with administered FX controls, New Zealand simply has no surrender requirement, no registration queue, no BOP coding approval, and no statutory matching of export receipts.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Not applicable. New Zealand imposes no statutory timeline, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no surrender obligation for export foreign currency receipts. Exporters may retain proceeds in onshore or offshore foreign currency accounts, convert to New Zealand dollars at their own discretion, or redeploy the proceeds for future platform payouts, provided the underlying transactions remain compliant with the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 and standard bank commercial terms.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Offshore digital e-money institutions such as Wise, Airwallex, and similar providers are not legally barred in New Zealand, but they are subject to the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008 and the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009. To service a New Zealand company, an EMI must register on the Financial Service Providers Register and maintain an approved dispute resolution scheme. However, an EMI should be treated only as a complementary clearing rail for high-frequency Steam and PlayStation payouts, not as the primary treasury backbone. A registered Tier 1 domestic commercial bank remains mandatory for capital verification, Companies Office evidence, IRD tax payments, RBNZ settlement liquidity, and the robust source-of-funds audit trail expected by auditors and the Inland Revenue Department. Feasibility rating: high as a payout-side convenience rail; low as a substitute for a New Zealand licensed bank account.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: New Zealand law does not require all directors to appear physically in a bank branch. Under the Companies Act 1993, the company must maintain a registered office in New Zealand and have at least one director resident in New Zealand or Australia under the statutory requirements. For a low-risk digital publishing entity, major New Zealand banks generally accept remote onboarding with video identification, certified passport copies, proof of business address, and a verified board resolution. Some banks may require an in-person interview with the New Zealand resident director or company secretary before activating the capital escrow account. Consular proxy opening is not a recognised New Zealand banking mechanism; the practical equivalent is remote online identity verification combined with a New Zealand registered agent or locally resident director who can attend if the bank's compliance committee requests enhanced due diligence.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Complex multi-layer beneficial ownership and nominee shareholding obscuring the ultimate beneficial owners of the New Zealand publishing company.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: A complete Companies Office extract; the official share register; certificates of incorporation for every legal entity in the ownership chain; any trust deed and trustee resolutions; source of wealth declarations; certified passports of every ultimate beneficial owner holding 25 percent or more; a written control chain diagram; and a notarised board resolution authorising the banking relationship.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Initial share capital injected from a non-resident shareholder where the source of funds is unclear or where third-party funding or crypto assets appear in the payment trail.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Six to twelve months of original bank statements for the transferring shareholder; audited financial statements or tax returns; statutory declarations of source of wealth and source of funds; a notarised share subscription agreement; a resolution of the board approving the equity issuance; the inward SWIFT MT103 confirmation with a clearly stated equity purpose; and evidence that the funds were received directly from the shareholder's own bank account, not through an unrelated intermediary.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Frequent near-identical digital store payouts from Valve and Sony Interactive Entertainment that could be mischaracterised as trade-based money laundering or unlicensed royalty processing.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed digital distribution agreements with Valve and Sony; monthly platform payout and royalty statements; game title sales and pricing reports; VAT and GST invoices; the licensing and publishing contract suite; treasury reconciliation reports mapping payout date, game title, territory, refunds, and platform fees; and a narrative memo explaining the revenue recognition model under IFRS.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctions and export control exposure arising from online game distribution, user-generated content, or publishing rights involving restricted territories and sanctioned parties.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: A written sanctions screening policy and screening logs; the geographical distribution and geo-blocking schedule approved by Valve and PlayStation; the platform terms confirming restricted storefronts; an export control classification memorandum prepared under United States, United Nations, and New Zealand sanctions frameworks; an IP due diligence report; and a legal opinion confirming the entity has no direct or indirect dealings with sanctioned persons or jurisdictions.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound equity capital should be routed by SWIFT MT103 from the non-resident shareholder's own corporate or personal bank account directly into the New Zealand company's NZD business transaction account with the payment narrative Equity Contribution, Share Subscription, or Application for Shares. The Overseas Investment Act 2005 consent is not required for a pure digital games publishing company unless sensitive land, significant business assets, or fishing quota form part of the transaction. The bank will require a board resolution, a completed foreign investment source-of-funds questionnaire, and a company ownership disclosure. After cleared funds arrive, the company must issue the shares, update the Companies Office shareholding record, and obtain an accountant's capital verification certificate evidencing the non-dilutive capital injection. Where a multi-currency account is used, the bank applies a standard commercial FX rate and no surrender or conversion approval is needed.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Steam Valve and PlayStation Store payouts should be settled through USD-denominated SWIFT MT103 transfers from the New Zealand company's multi-currency account to the platform's designated bank account, using the platform reference and royalty invoice numbers in the payment details. For physical collector editions and retail merchandise, clearing rails should include irrevocable confirmed commercial letters of credit for large batch production, documentary collections for moderate-value shipments, and SWIFT direct transfers for smaller purchase orders. The company may maintain a USD account to reduce FX conversion friction, convert only when commercial rates are advantageous, and use the same clearing rails to pay third-party game developers, sub-licensors, audio vendors, and overseas marketing agencies. All outward payments must include a matching invoice, contract, or platform settlement statement to satisfy bank monitoring and New Zealand source-of-funds rules.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Plain vanilla FX forwards and FX swaps with an RBNZ-registered bank or authorised derivatives dealer, matched to forecast Steam and PlayStation royalty inflows, with tenors aligned to the platform payout cycle and board-approved treasury limits.

Cross-currency swaps and currency options are permissible for longer-term balance-sheet hedging of intercompany loans, royalty obligations, or multi-year distribution guarantees, provided the hedge is supported by a signed underlying commercial contract, is not speculative, and is reported under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 conduct and disclosure rules.

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) are permitted as a secondary hedge for emerging-market payout currencies that cannot be physically delivered in New Zealand, but they must be backed by a specific sales contract or platform receivable and must not be used to evade New Zealand or international sanctions.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (Registrar of Companies)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annual filing based on the incorporation anniversary; the filing window opens 20 working days before the anniversary and the return must be filed within 20 working days after the anniversary date.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: If not filed by the statutory deadline, the Registrar issues a notice of default; failure to remedy within a further 20 working days exposes the company to procedural removal from the New Zealand register. Company directors may be liable to fines of up to NZ$10,000, and continued non-compliance leads to strike-off and dissolution.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: IR4 Company Annual Income Tax Return
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For a 31 March balance date, the return is due by 7 July following the end of the tax year; for a non-standard balance date, the due date is the 7th day of the 4th month after the balance date, subject to applicable tax-agent extension rules.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalties apply after the due date, together with IRD late payment penalties of 1% per month on unpaid tax and prescribed use-of-money interest; continued non-compliance can trigger enforcement action and director liability.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Filing of Audited Financial Statements and Auditor's Report where the company is a large company or otherwise subject to a statutory audit
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (Registrar of Companies)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 20 working days after the financial statements are signed and dated by the directors; the auditor's report must be delivered with the audited financial statements where audit is mandatory.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file audited financial statements where required constitutes an offence under the Financial Reporting Act 2013 and Companies Act 1993; directors are liable to fines not exceeding NZ$10,000 per default and the company may be subject to adverse register action.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: A mandatory independent statutory audit is required if the company is an issuer, has public accountability, is otherwise required by its constitution or shareholder resolution, or meets the New Zealand 'large company' size tests. A company is large for the reporting period in question if it satisfies at least one of: (a) total assets exceed NZ$60 million; (b) total revenue exceeds NZ$30 million; or (c) 100 or more full-time-equivalent employees; measurements apply on a group consolidated basis where applicable. A small or medium private company can generally waive audit by unanimous shareholder resolution, but shareholders holding at least 5% of voting rights may require an audit to be undertaken.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: New Zealand Generally Accepted Accounting Practice (NZ GAAP) as prescribed by the New Zealand Accounting Standards Board (XRB): Tier 1 large entities apply NZ IFRS (New Zealand equivalents to International Financial Reporting Standards); Tier 2 entities apply NZ IFRS with Reduced Disclosure Regime (NZ IFRS RDR); eligible smaller for-profit entities may use the simplified small-entity reporting framework permitted by XRB standards.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: New Zealand does not maintain a public beneficial-ownership register for ordinary private companies. Ownership is confirmed annually through the Companies Office Annual Return, which must record current shareholders, share classes, and share numbers. New share allotments must be filed with the Registrar of Companies within 20 working days of allotment. Transfers of existing shares must be recorded in the company's Register of Members immediately upon lodgement and are not centrally filed with the Registrar; the updated ownership position is reflected in the next Annual Return. Changes to director details must also be notified within 20 working days. There is no general 30-day UBO reporting window in New Zealand corporate law for private limited companies; AML/CFT beneficial-ownership records are maintained separately by financial-service reporting entities where applicable.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Minute Book containing shareholder resolutions, board minutes, and company decisions

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: $200 - $500 per year for a registered office and professional corporate secretarial agent in New Zealand
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: $700 - $2,500 per year for a certified independent audit of a typically sized New Zealand private company, subject to group, complexity, and reporting requirements

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No general patent box or free-zone preferential regime; R&D tax credit of 15% available for qualifying New Zealand software development and game production expenditure; immediate expensing of low-value assets (under NZD 5,000) and certain digital intangibles; no foreign dividend exemption for non-resident portfolio dividends unless held via an attributed CFC in a high-tax jurisdiction; the standard 28% rate applies to resident company worldwide income with foreign tax credits available.
corporate_income_tax_regime.tax_loss_carryforward_limit_years: Unlimited (subject to a 49% continuous ownership test under Income Tax Act 2007 s IA 5)

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 – Company Income Tax Return (electronically filed through Inland Revenue's myIR portal; paper filing also accepted but discouraged)
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual (final return filed once per income year; provisional tax paid in three instalments or via the GST ratio method)
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: For a standard 31 March balance date, the IR4 must be filed by 7 July. Tax agents may obtain an extension to the following 31 March for clients with pre-approved filing schedules; a terminal tax due date generally aligns with 7 April of the following year if the balance date is 31 March.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross income: all New Zealand and worldwide revenue from digital game publishing, including Steam, PlayStation Store, Epic Games Store, Xbox, and in-game microtransactions, after deducting platform commission fees (if shown gross) but before expenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: As NZ Ltd is tax-resident in New Zealand, report all global sales revenue. Do not net off royalty payments to third-party IP holders or platform distribution fees in Box 1; those are deductible expenses in Box 2. If the company is a non-resident entity with a fixed base in New Zealand, only New Zealand-sourced income is taxable; Steam/PS store sales to New Zealand customers may generate attributable income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total deductible expenses: game development costs, outsourcing fees, platform commissions, marketing, employee salaries, rent, depreciation, amortisation of intangibles, and intercompany fees paid at arm's length.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Expenses must satisfy the general deductibility test (Income Tax Act 2007 s DA 1) and not be capital in nature. Intercompany royalties for IP licensing from offshore affiliates must be supported by an OECD-compliant transfer pricing analysis; otherwise the deduction may be disallowed and penalties applied. Non-resident companies performing all game development offshore cannot allocate those costs against NZ-sourced revenue unless properly structured as service fees.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net taxable income before adjustments: Box 1 minus Box 2.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If net income is negative, a loss is claimed; loss carryforward rules apply subject to shareholder continuity. For non-resident companies, ensure that only New Zealand-sourced expenses are deducted; global overhead allocation should be made on a reasonable basis.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax adjustments: add back non-deductible fines, entertainment expenses exceeding limits, interest on shareholder loans not at arm's length, transfer pricing upward adjustments, and any disallowed foreign taxes.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Include transfer pricing adjustments for any intercompany transactions not at arm's length. For non-resident entities, adjustments may also arise under the thin capitalisation rules if debt-to-asset ratios exceed the allowable threshold (usually 60% for non-resident owned entities). Cross-border gaming royalties must be benchmarked.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income after loss carryforward: apply available loss offsets from prior years, subject to continuity of ownership, to arrive at income subject to tax.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the company has foreign shareholders and ownership changes by more than 51%, losses lapse. Non-resident owners contemplating restructuring must first trace continuity. For treaty purposes, ensure that any loss utilization does not create a sham or avoidance transaction.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Income tax payable: apply the 28% corporate rate to Box 5, then subtract R&D tax credits, foreign tax credits, provisional tax already paid, and any imputation credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident shareholders receiving dividends will have New Zealand imputation credits attached; foreign tax credits are limited to New Zealand tax on foreign-source income. Do not subtract NRWT from corporate tax payable; NRWT is a separate liability imposed on distributions. Ensure provisional tax paid is reconciled to avoid late payment penalties.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing of IR4 triggers an immediate non-compliance penalty of NZD 250, plus NZD 50 for each additional month the return remains overdue, capped at NZD 500. Late payment of terminal tax attracts an initial late payment penalty of 1% of the unpaid tax, followed by an additional 4% after 7 days, then a 1% penalty for each subsequent month. Interest on underpayments accrues daily at the IRD use-of-money rate (currently 9.18% per annum for over-due tax). Evasion, fraud or wilful misrepresentation can lead to civil shortfall penalties up to 150% of the resulting tax shortfall and criminal prosecution with fines up to NZD 50,000 and imprisonment for up to 5 years.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: Non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) on dividends paid by NZ Ltd to non-resident shareholders is 30%. If the dividend is fully imputed (i.e., carries new Zealand imputation credits), the NRWT rate is reduced to 15%. Under most bilateral double tax treaties, a qualified holding of 10% or more may attract a 5% dividend rate, with 15% applying to portfolio holdings; the exact rate depends on the shareholder's country of residence.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke DTA relief on outbound dividends, interest, or royalties, the non-resident payee must obtain an official Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) from its home jurisdiction's tax authority and provide a completed New Zealand Inland Revenue declaration (IR67 series or country-specific certificate) confirming residency and beneficial ownership (no nominee or conduit arrangement). The payer must retain the TRC and beneficial ownership statement before applying the lower treaty withholding rate. If excessive NRWT is withheld at source, the non-resident may file a refund claim with Inland Revenue, supplying the full documentation chain and proof of payment, within the statutory time bar (generally 4 years).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Interest: statutory NRWT is 15% on interest paid to non-residents; an approved issuer levy (AIL) of 2% may substitute for NRWT only if the lender is non-associate, interest is not payable to a related person, and the approved issuer status is maintained. Royalties: statutory NRWT on cross-border royalties (including video game licensing, IP, and software rights) is 15%. Under applicable DTAs, royalty rates are commonly reduced to between 5% and 10%, and interest to 0% to 10%, depending on the treaty partner. Domestic anti-avoidance rules can recharacterise excessive or artificial royalty payments as dividends.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Mandatory Master File and Local File are required for multinational groups with consolidated group revenue exceeding NZD 1.2 billion. In addition, any cross-border related-party transaction with an aggregate value exceeding NZD 10 million in an income year triggers a statutory obligation to prepare and retain contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation evidencing arm's length pricing. Even below the NZD 10 million threshold, a taxpayer must still be able to demonstrate arm's length compliance on request.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not apply OECD-style Economic Substance Regulations akin to offshore financial centres, but the 'economic substance over legal form' principle drives the general anti-avoidance rule (Income Tax Act 2007 s BG 1) and the place of effective management (POEM) test for tax residency. NZ Ltd must have real staff, office premises, decision-making powers, and active game-publishing functions in New Zealand. If the board of directors and core income-generating activities (CIGA) for publishing, platform contracts, and IP exploitation are located outside New Zealand, Inland Revenue may re-characterise the entity as non-resident or attribute profits to the foreign head office, and a non-resident company using a New Zealand shell without real substance may be ignored for tax purposes.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion – Undisclosed Offshore Digital Revenue
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Directing Steam/PlayStation sales proceeds into an offshore nominee account, failing to record worldwide revenue on the IR4, or deliberately omitting microtransaction and DLC income generated from digital storefronts. This includes using a foreign e-wallet that is not disclosed to Inland Revenue and not reflected in the company's financial statements.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Breach of the Tax Administration Act 1994 ss 141 and 143B (evasion or similar act); shortfall penalty of up to 150% of the tax evaded; criminal conviction under s 143A carries imprisonment for up to 5 years and fines up to NZD 50,000 for the company, with liability for the tax, interest, and penalties.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who directed, authorised, or acquiesced in the concealment can be held jointly and severally liable under s 149 of the Tax Administration Act for the company's unpaid tax and penalties; civil asset restitution and freezing orders may issue; directors face individual criminal prosecution, disqualification from managing companies under s 383 of the Companies Act 1993, and imprisonment for up to 5 years. Departure prohibition orders can prevent overseas travel pending resolution.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Manipulation in Cross-Border Royalties
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying an offshore affiliated holding company an inflated royalty for 'brand support' or 'IP licensing' without economic merit, or selling digital game rights to a related party in a zero-tax jurisdiction at below-market prices, thereby stripping New Zealand profit and failing to maintain contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation despite intercompany payments exceeding NZD 10 million.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Income Tax Act 2007 ss GC 6 to GC 14 empower the IRD to adjust taxable income to arm's length; transfer pricing shortfall penalties range from 20% (failure to exercise reasonable care) to 40% (unacceptable tax position) and up to 150% if conduct amounts to evasion or fraud; late payment interest accrues; the adjustment eliminates any tax benefit and may also trigger dividend recharacterisation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign false transfer pricing documentation or knowingly understate taxable income are personally liable for the tax shortfall and penalties; under the Companies Act 1993, they may be liable for reckless trading if the arrangement deprives creditors of assets; criminal liability for tax evasion can result in imprisonment up to 5 years, blacklisting for director appointments, and joint and several recovery from personal assets.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Improper Avoidance of Non-Resident Withholding Tax
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Structuring outbound profit repatriation as 'repayment of a bogus loan', 'service fee', or 'reimbursed expenses' to avoid dividend or royalty NRWT; alternatively, claiming a reduced DTA rate on dividends/royalties without obtaining a valid Tax Residency Certificate and beneficial ownership declaration, thereby failing to withhold the proper 15% or 30% NRWT.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Non-resident withholding tax rules under Income Tax Act 2007 ss RD 10-RD 27, RE 13, and RF 2 require withholding on dividends, interest, and royalties. Failure to withhold triggers a shortfall penalty of up to 150% of the unpaid NRWT plus interest; the general anti-avoidance rule (s BG 1) can recharacterise the payment as a dividend; the company is liable for the unpaid NRWT as a deemed trustee, and criminal sanctions apply for deliberate evasion under s 143A of the Tax Administration Act.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are personally liable for NRWT the company fails to deduct and remit, because the amounts are held in trust for Inland Revenue; Inland Revenue may issue notices to directors for asset attachment and personal recovery; failure to comply can lead to contempt of court, travel bans (departure prohibition orders), civil restitution, disqualification as a director, and imprisonment for up to 5 years for fraudulent evasion. Piercing the corporate veil is permitted where the company is a mere façade for the shareholder/director's tax avoidance scheme.
